words.definition: The luck of stumbling on something valuable while looking for nothing in particular.
words.example: Meeting my future business partner in that delayed airport line was pure serendipity.
words.mnemonic: From the fairy tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip,' who kept making lucky discoveries; hear 'serene dip' into good fortune.

words.definition: Occurring by a fortunate accident rather than by plan.
words.example: Their serendipitous meeting at the library grew into a lifelong friendship.
words.mnemonic: Adjective of the Serendip tale — a 'serene dip' that turns out lucky.

words.definition: The quality of happening by accident rather than intention.
words.example: By sheer fortuity, the two scientists arrived at the same formula on the same day.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'fortuna' (luck) — picture Fortune pouring you a cup of tea you never asked for.

words.definition: Happening at just the right moment, as though guided by a benevolent higher power.
words.example: The providential arrival of the rescue boat saved the stranded hikers.
words.mnemonic: 'Provide' + '-ential' — as if a divine hand provides exactly what you need, right on time.

words.definition: Benevolent guardianship, attributed to God or fate, believed to steer events toward good.
words.example: She trusted that providence would see her family through the harsh winter.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'providere,' to see ahead — a foreseeing power that 'provides' for the future.

words.definition: Strikingly well suited to the occasion; aptly and gracefully expressed.
words.example: The toast ended on a felicitous phrase that had the whole room smiling.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'Felix,' Latin for happy — a felicitous remark makes everyone Felix-glad.

words.definition: A state of great joy, or skillful aptness in wording.
words.example: She described the sunset with such felicity that no one wanted her to stop.
words.mnemonic: 'Felix' means happy; Felicity is the woman who is pure happiness.

words.definition: Something helpful given as a favor or great advantage.
words.example: The new well proved a boon to the drought-stricken village.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'boom' — a boon gives your day a sudden boom of good.

words.definition: Riches viewed with contempt, seen as dishonestly or shamefully gained.
words.example: He cared nothing for honor, chasing only pelf and the power it bought.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pelt' — grabbing furs for filthy cash; shabby loot for a selfish 'pelf'.

words.definition: Determined by the roll of the dice rather than by skill or plan.
words.example: The composer added aleatory passages where the musicians improvise freely.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'alea' = dice (Caesar's 'alea iacta est,' the die is cast) — aleatory is dice-y.

words.definition: Governed by probability, so outcomes vary unpredictably from one instance to the next.
words.example: The model treats stock prices as a stochastic process driven by random shocks.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'stokhos,' to aim or guess — a 'stock-astic' guess at a moving target.

words.definition: A circumstance that comes about by chance rather than by plan.
words.example: It was mere happenstance that both of them chose the same remote café.
words.mnemonic: Blend of 'happen' + 'circumstance' — a circumstance that just happens to happen.

words.definition: An uncertain situation that may or may not occur, requiring a backup plan.
words.example: The budget set aside funds for any contingency, from floods to strikes.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'contingere,' to touch or befall — a future 'con-tinged' with uncertainty.

words.definition: Dependent on something else that may or may not happen.
words.example: Her promotion is contingent on the merger going through next month.
words.mnemonic: 'Con-TINGE-ent' — one outcome is tinged by, and touches, a condition it depends on.

words.definition: Arising by chance from an outside source rather than naturally belonging.
words.example: The scar was adventitious, a result of the accident and not something he was born with.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'advent'/'adventure' (Latin 'advenire,' to arrive) — it just arrives from outside.

words.definition: A sudden, impulsive change of mind or behavior with no clear reason.
words.example: On a caprice, she quit her job and booked a one-way flight to Peru.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'capra' (goat) — picture a goat leaping about unpredictably, springing wherever the mood takes it.

words.definition: Likely to change often; not steady, loyal, or dependable.
words.example: His inconstant affections meant no relationship of his ever lasted more than a month.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + constant (steady) = not staying the same.

words.definition: Giving the impression that something bad is about to happen.
words.example: Ominous black clouds massed over the ridge just as we started the long hike.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'omen' — an ominous sky is an omen of doom.

words.definition: A strong feeling that something, usually bad, is about to happen.
words.example: She had a premonition of disaster and, at the gate, refused to board the plane.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + monition (a warning) = a warning felt before the event.

words.definition: A person or source believed to give wise counsel or foretell the future.
words.example: Before any major campaign, the king traveled to the temple to consult the oracle.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'or-a-clue' — someone who always hands you a clue about what's coming.

words.definition: Accurately describing or foretelling events before they occur.
words.example: His prophetic warning about the market crash came true almost exactly two years later.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro-phone' — like getting a phone call straight from the future.

words.definition: To foretell or prophesy what is going to happen.
words.example: The old astrologer claimed he could vaticinate the fates of every newborn prince.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'Vatican' — picture a robed figure at the Vatican solemnly foretelling the future.

words.definition: Having major, often disastrous, consequences for what comes after.
words.example: It was a fateful decision to set sail that morning, despite every storm warning.
words.mnemonic: 'fate' + '-ful' = full of destiny — a moment loaded with what's to come.

words.definition: To decide or settle an outcome in advance, especially by a higher power.
words.example: The theologians argued that God had foreordained the destiny of every soul.
words.mnemonic: fore- (before) + ordain (to decree) = to decree it beforehand.

words.definition: To settle someone's future or outcome in advance by a controlling power.
words.example: In the novel, the separated twins seem predestined to meet again exactly ten years later.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + destine (destination) = your destination fixed before you even set out.

words.definition: The quality of being impossible to avoid or prevent.
words.example: Once the deadline slipped, the layoffs took on a grim inevitability nobody could deny.
words.mnemonic: in- (not) + Latin 'evitare' (to avoid) = the state of not being avoidable.

words.definition: A serious event that causes great damage, suffering, or distress.
words.example: The flood was the worst calamity the valley had endured in over a century.
words.mnemonic: Think 'Calamity Jane' — the frontier figure forever surrounded by trouble and disaster.

words.definition: Causing serious damage, suffering, or ruin.
words.example: The general's calamitous retreat through the mountains cost thousands of lives.
words.mnemonic: The adjective of 'Calamity Jane' — anything as trouble-prone and ruinous as she was.

words.definition: A sudden event causing great suffering or widespread destruction.
words.example: The tanker's spill became an environmental catastrophe that fouled the entire coastline.
words.mnemonic: Greek kata- (down) + strophe (turning) — a sudden, sharp turn downward into ruin.

words.definition: A violent, large-scale disaster or dramatic upheaval.
words.example: The eruption was a cataclysm that buried three cities under scorching ash overnight.
words.mnemonic: Greek kata- (down) + klyzein (to wash) — a great flood washing everything away, like the biblical deluge.

words.definition: Relating to a sudden, violent event causing great destruction or dramatic change.
words.example: When the dam burst, the cataclysmic flood swept away entire villages within minutes.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'cata-CLASH-mic' — a colossal clash that smashes everything to pieces.

words.definition: A sudden, total, and often humiliating collapse or failure of an event or plan.
words.example: The product launch was a debacle: the demo crashed, the mic died, and reporters walked out.
words.mnemonic: 'DE-BACK-le' — the whole thing falls flat on its BACK and breaks apart (French for the breaking-up of ice).

words.definition: A difficult situation full of hardship, misfortune, or trouble.
words.example: Growing up in poverty, she faced constant adversity but never lost her ambition.
words.mnemonic: 'AD-VERSE-ity' — when life's verses turn against you, everything feels adverse.

words.definition: A period of great trouble, suffering, or distress.
words.example: After years of tribulation in exile, the refugees finally found safety and peace.
words.mnemonic: 'TRIBE-ulation' — picture an entire tribe crushed under waves of misery (Latin 'tribulum', a threshing sledge that grinds grain).

words.definition: Painful, exhausting labor or a very distressing experience.
words.example: The travail of hauling supplies up the mountain in a blizzard left the team frostbitten.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'travel' — but grueling travel, backbreaking toil (French 'travail' = work).

words.definition: A condition of ongoing pain, illness, or suffering.
words.example: Chronic migraines were an affliction that kept her bedridden for days each month.
words.mnemonic: 'a-FLICK-tion' — each flick brings a sting that keeps hurting and won't let go.

words.definition: A cause of persistent harm, ruin, or annoyance.
words.example: Slow traffic on the bridge was the bane of his morning commute.
words.mnemonic: Think of Batman's villain BANE — he rhymes with 'pain' and brings nothing but ruin.

words.definition: Menacing and threatening, seeming to promise evil or harm.
words.example: The wolf fixed the lamb with a baleful stare before it lunged.
words.mnemonic: 'BALE-ful' — a full BALE (bundle) of bad omens; a wailful, hateful glare.

words.definition: Causing serious harm, destruction, or death; poisonous in effect.
words.example: The baneful runoff leaked into the river, killing every fish downstream.
words.mnemonic: Full of 'bane' (poison) — like baneberry, a toxic plant; rhymes with 'painful'.

words.definition: A long, mournful complaint or bitter lament about society's woes.
words.example: His toast dissolved into a jeremiad about how the younger generation had ruined everything.
words.mnemonic: Named for the prophet JEREMIAH, whose biblical Lamentations were one long sorrowful wail.

words.definition: A person or thing that causes great and widespread suffering or devastation.
words.example: Malaria remains a scourge across many tropical regions, claiming countless lives each year.
words.mnemonic: 'SCOUR' + 'urge' — an urge to whip and scour the land bare (a scourge was literally a whip).

words.definition: A dangerous, difficult, or unfortunate situation someone is stuck in.
words.example: The news coverage highlighted the plight of families left homeless by the earthquake.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'blight' and 'tight' — you're wedged in a tight, blighted spot.

words.definition: An unlucky or unfortunate incident, especially one arising from a risky undertaking.
words.example: Their camping trip became a misadventure when the tent blew away and the map got soaked.
words.mnemonic: 'mis-' (badly) + 'adventure' — an outing that goes hilariously or dangerously wrong.

words.definition: An instance of bad luck or an unlucky accident.
words.example: By some mischance, both elevators failed on the very morning of his big interview.
words.mnemonic: 'mis-' (bad) + 'chance' — a chance outcome that turned out badly.

words.definition: A small unlucky accident that causes minor trouble.
words.example: A wardrobe mishap left him with a coffee stain right before the presentation.
words.mnemonic: 'mis-' + 'hap' — 'hap' is old English for luck (as in 'happen'), so a bad hap.

words.definition: Causing severe damage, collapse, or financial disaster.
words.example: The lawsuit's ruinous legal fees forced the small bakery to close its doors.
words.mnemonic: It literally holds 'ruin' — something ruinous leaves you in ruins.

words.definition: A person or thing believed to bring bad luck.
words.example: Every time he wears that hat to a game his team loses — he's a total jinx.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'sphinx': a mysterious, riddling curse hanging over you.

words.definition: A spoken wish that harm come to someone.
words.example: The old witch hurled a malediction at the knight, swearing he would never see home again.
words.mnemonic: 'mal-' (bad) + 'diction' (speech) = bad speech aimed at you.

words.definition: A shouted or muttered appeal for evil to fall on another.
words.example: He stormed off the pitch, hurling imprecations at the referee who had ejected him.
words.mnemonic: 'im-' + '-prec-' (to pray) = praying badly against someone.

words.definition: A person or thing that is intensely disliked or formally condemned.
words.example: To a lifelong vegetarian, a steak dinner is complete anathema.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-NASTY-ma' — a nasty thing you can't stand.

words.definition: The act of loudly condemning or detesting someone or something.
words.example: The tyrant's name is now spoken only with execration by the people he oppressed.
words.mnemonic: 'exe-' + 'cremation' — you'd gladly burn what you utterly loathe.

words.definition: A rival or force that consistently causes someone's defeat or punishment.
words.example: The detective finally cornered his lifelong nemesis in an abandoned warehouse.
words.mnemonic: Named for Nemesis, the Greek goddess of retribution.

words.definition: The cause of a person's ruin or collapse.
words.example: His arrogance proved to be his undoing when every investor abandoned the company.
words.mnemonic: To 'undo' a knot is to unravel it — your undoing unravels you.

words.definition: A sudden loss of power, wealth, or status.
words.example: Greed led to the emperor's downfall, and his realm crumbled within a year.
words.mnemonic: Picture a king plunging down off the top of his own tower.

words.definition: A deserved punishment or fate that someone finally receives.
words.example: The schoolyard bully got his comeuppance when the smallest kid stood up to him.
words.mnemonic: What's 'coming up' to you — your just deserts arriving at last.

words.definition: Complete and everlasting spiritual ruin; hell.
words.example: The preacher warned that a life of cruelty leads straight to perdition.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'perdere', to lose utterly — the ultimate total loss.

words.definition: Having persistent misfortune; never favored by chance.
words.example: The luckless gambler lost his last coin on a bet that missed by a single number.
words.mnemonic: 'luck' + '-less' = stripped of every scrap of luck.

words.definition: Surrounded by troubles or attackers; under constant pressure.
words.example: The beleaguered manager faced complaints from staff, customers, and investors all at once.
words.mnemonic: 'be-' + 'leaguer' (a besieging camp) — an army pitches tents all around you.

words.definition: Deserving sorrow or regret; unfortunate and disappointing.
words.example: The team's lamentable performance left the coach shaking his head in dismay.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'lament' inside it — something you cry and mourn over.

words.definition: Unexpected and inconvenient, awkward, or inappropriate.
words.example: Nothing untoward happened during the flight, and the passengers landed calmly and on time.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' + 'toward' — events not heading toward the way they should.

words.definition: Full of danger or risk; dangerously uncertain and difficult to escape.
words.example: After three failed harvests, the village finances were in a parlous state.
words.mnemonic: It's literally a worn-down form of 'perilous' — say it fast and you hear 'per'lous.'

words.definition: Not securely held or in position; likely to fall or fail at any moment.
words.example: He balanced the last book on the precarious stack, and the whole tower wobbled.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pray-carious' — a position so shaky you can only pray it holds.

words.definition: Extremely serious or severe, causing great suffering or sorrow.
words.example: The surgeon warned that any further delay could inflict grievous harm.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'grieve' — a grievous wound is one bad enough to make you grieve.

words.definition: Full of or expressing deep sadness and mournful distress.
words.example: The cello's dolorous notes filled the hall like a slow funeral procession.
words.mnemonic: Spanish 'dolor' means pain or grief — dolorous is simply overflowing with dolor.

words.definition: Showing regret or sorrow, often with a wry, self-aware smile.
words.example: She gave a rueful laugh when she spotted the typo on her book's cover.
words.mnemonic: To 'rue' something is to regret it — so rueful is a face that's full of rue.

words.definition: Producing a good or beneficial effect, often through an unwelcome warning or lesson.
words.example: The near-miss on the icy highway had a salutary effect on his driving.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'salus' (health), same root as 'salute' — it toasts to your wellbeing.

words.definition: Help and relief given to someone in distress or great difficulty.
words.example: The lifeboat crew brought succor to the sailors stranded on the wreck.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'succurrere,' to run up and help — picture a rescuer sprinting toward the fallen.

words.definition: A confused, complicated, and often embarrassing situation or disagreement.
words.example: The mayor resigned amid the imbroglio over misspent city funds.
words.mnemonic: Say 'im-BROIL-io' — everyone caught in it is stuck in one hot, tangled broil.

words.definition: To contribute significantly to someone's credit or shame, or to rebound back upon them.
words.example: Her quiet generosity redounded to the honor of the entire family.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'rebound' inside it — from Latin 'redundare,' to surge back onto its source.

words.definition: To fill with water and sink, or to fail completely and collapse.
words.example: The overloaded ferry foundered just minutes after leaving the harbor.
words.mnemonic: Don't confuse it with 'flounder' — think 'found' at the bottom: a ship going to the sea floor.

description: advanced and low-frequency — fortune and misfortune
